title: Odds and the S-Curve
subtitle: how risk factors become a probability
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E02_OddsAndTheSCurve

segments.visual: Last episode's patient, with three risk-factor tags, above a probability ruler from 0 to 100%.

sentences.text: Last time, we ended with a wish: one ruler for risk, where everything we know about a patient turns into a single probability.

segments.visual: The chip settles on the ruler at 20%.

sentences.text: Here's the obvious way to build it.
Start a typical patient at 20%, then add points for each risk factor.
sentences.say: Start a typical patient at twenty percent, then add points for each risk factor.

segments.visual: Each tag drops in and the chip hops right: 45%, 75%, then off the end of the ruler.

sentences.text: Age 81: plus 25. Diabetes: plus 30. A third hospital stay this year: plus 35.
sentences.say: Age eighty-one: plus twenty-five. Diabetes: plus thirty. A third hospital stay this year: plus thirty-five.

segments.visual: The chip hangs past the end of the ruler at 110%, marked in coral.

sentences.text: That's 110%.
sentences.say: That's a hundred and ten percent.

sentences.text: A probability can't do that. Adding points was the wrong move, on the wrong ruler.

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: odds, and the curve that turns any patient into a probability.

segments.visual: Ten chips in a row; two fill.

sentences.text: Let's try a different ruler.
Take ten patients who each have a 20% chance of coming back. On average, two do, and eight don't.
sentences.say: Take ten patients who each have a twenty percent chance of coming back. On average, two do, and eight don't.

segments.visual: A bracket over all ten: probability 20%. Then the two set against the eight: odds 1 to 4.

sentences.text: Probability compares the two with all ten.
Odds compare the two with the eight: one to four, or a quarter.

segments.visual: A probability ruler and an odds ruler with linked markers; the chips refill to five, then eight.

sentences.text: At 50%, it's five against five: odds of one.
sentences.say: At fifty percent, it's five against five: odds of one.

sentences.text: At 80%, eight against two: odds of four.
sentences.say: At eighty percent, eight against two: odds of four.

segments.visual: The probability marker creeps toward 100% while the odds marker runs off the end: 9, 99, 999.

sentences.text: And as the probability creeps toward 100%, the odds just keep running: 9, 99, 999.
sentences.say: And as the probability creeps toward one hundred percent, the odds just keep running: nine, ninety-nine, nine hundred and ninety-nine.

sentences.text: This ruler has no ceiling.

segments.visual: On the odds ruler, the short stretch from 0 to 1 is bracketed: everyone below fifty-fifty.

sentences.text: But it's a lopsided ruler.
Every patient below fifty-fifty is squeezed between zero and one, while everyone above gets all the room in the world.

segments.visual: A copy of the ruler stretches: the ticks at 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4 slide until they are evenly spaced.

sentences.text: The cure is a logarithm.
On a log scale, every doubling of the odds is one equal step: a quarter, a half, one, two, four.

segments.visual: Three rulers stacked: probability, odds, log-odds, with one patient tracked on all three at 50%, 20% and 80%.

sentences.text: This is the log-odds ruler. Fifty-fifty sits at zero.
20% is about minus 1.4, and 80% is plus 1.4: perfectly symmetric.
sentences.say: Twenty percent is about minus one point four, and eighty percent is plus one point four: perfectly symmetric.

segments.visual: The patient slides far left and far right; the log-odds ruler never ends.

sentences.text: And it runs forever in both directions. No floor, no ceiling, nothing to bump into.

segments.visual: A yellow arrow of length 1.39 on the log-odds ruler.

sentences.text: Here's why that matters. On the log-odds ruler, a risk factor is simply a step.
Take one that multiplies the odds by four: a step of 1.4 to the right.
sentences.say: Take one that multiplies the odds by four: a step of one point four to the right.

segments.visual: Four patients at 5%, 20%, 50% and 80% each take the same step on the log-odds ruler.

sentences.text: Now give that same step to four different patients.

segments.visual: On the probability ruler their jumps appear one by one: +12, +30, +30, +14 points.

sentences.text: On the probability ruler, 5% becomes 17%. 20% becomes 50%. 50% becomes 80%. And 80% becomes 94%.
sentences.say: On the probability ruler, five percent becomes seventeen. Twenty becomes fifty. Fifty becomes eighty. And eighty becomes ninety-four.

segments.visual: The four equal yellow steps pulse, then the four unequal jumps; the 100% end stays untouched.

sentences.text: Same step, very different jumps: big in the middle, small near the ends.
And nobody ever goes past one hundred.

segments.visual: Axes: earlier hospital stays along the bottom, log-odds up the side. Nine dots climb in equal steps.

sentences.text: Now picture a risk factor that comes in amounts, like the number of earlier hospital stays.
Suppose each extra stay is one more equal step in log-odds.

segments.visual: A straight line through the dots; a yellow slope triangle labelled beta.

sentences.text: On this scale, the pattern is a straight line. Its slope is the size of the step, and we'll call it beta.

segments.visual: The vertical axis becomes probability; the dots move and the line bends into an S.

sentences.text: Now switch the vertical axis back to probability.
The line bends into an S: steep in the middle, flat at both ends, and always between zero and one.

segments.visual: A tangent slides along the curve; a bar shows p(1 - p), longest at 50%.

sentences.text: How steep it is depends on where you stand. The steepness is proportional to p times one minus p: greatest at fifty-fifty, fading to nothing at the ends.
Keep that in your pocket. It comes back when we fit the model.

segments.visual: A yellow beta dial turns and the S steepens; then the curve slides left and right.

sentences.text: Turn beta up, and the S gets steeper.
Shift the starting point, and the whole curve slides sideways.

segments.visual: Cedar's twenty chips in two blocks of ten: 2 filled on the left, 6 on the right.

sentences.text: Let's fit one of these by hand. Remember Cedar?
Ten lower-risk patients, 2 readmitted. Ten higher-risk patients, 6 readmitted.
sentences.say: Ten lower-risk patients, two readmitted. Ten higher-risk patients, six readmitted.

segments.visual: Under each block: 2 : 8, odds 0.25; and 6 : 4, odds 1.5.

sentences.text: So the odds are 2 to 8, a quarter; and 6 to 4, one and a half.
sentences.say: So the odds are two to eight, a quarter; and six to four, one and a half.

segments.visual: Between them: times 6, the odds ratio.

sentences.text: Divide one by the other, and you get an odds ratio of six. At Cedar, higher risk multiplies the odds by six.

segments.visual: A log-odds ruler: a chip at -1.39, a yellow step of 1.79 to +0.41; the model written underneath.

sentences.text: On the log-odds ruler, that's a step of 1.79, starting from minus 1.39.
sentences.say: On the log-odds ruler, that's a step of one point seven nine, starting from minus one point three nine.

sentences.text: Those two numbers are a complete logistic model of Cedar.

segments.visual: Between the two probabilities: times 3. The 6 and the 3 sit one above the other.

sentences.text: One caution. Six times the odds is not six times the risk.
Cedar's rate went from 20% to 60%: three times, not six.
sentences.say: Cedar's rate went from twenty percent to sixty: three times, not six.

segments.visual: The patient again, on two rulers: probability above, log-odds below; a faded 110% past the end.

sentences.text: Now, back to our patient. This time, we add on the right ruler.

segments.visual: Three yellow steps stack on the log-odds ruler; the probability marker moves 45%, 77%, 94%.

sentences.text: Each risk factor is a step in log-odds, and the steps simply stack, one after another.

segments.visual: 94% lights up; the old 110% is struck through.

sentences.text: And the probability? 94%.
High, but still a probability.

segments.visual: The chip gains a shaded slice of 94%; chips with 20% and 50% slices appear beside it.

sentences.text: From now on, every chip carries its probability with it, as a shaded slice.
A sliver for a low-risk patient; nearly the whole disc for this one.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
Odds compare the patients who come back with those who don't.
Log-odds is the ruler where risk factors add.
And the S-curve carries the sum back to a probability.

segments.visual: Cedar's twenty chips, each with its slice; the slices pour into one bar: expected 8.0.

sentences.text: So now every patient has a probability.
Add them up across a clinic, and you get a number of patients: the readmissions we should expect.

segments.visual: Beside the bar, Cedar's eight filled chips: observed. Next episode title.

sentences.text: Next time, we'll set that number beside what actually happened. Observed, versus expected.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
